name: Ancient Hebrew
confidence_why: Gesenius-Kautzsch 1910, Prince 1975, McCarthy 1979 and Suchard 2016 all put main stress on the final syllable as a rule and on the penult in a bounded set of vowel-final forms, and Khan 2020 confirms that the Masoretic accents mark stress, but Suchard 2016 treats the surface position as phonemic (qåmǻ 'standing' vs qǻmå 'she stood up') where Prince 1975 and McCarthy 1979 derive the same forms by rule from underlying representations, so the placement is secure while the weight-conditioned analysis is only partly supported.

sweep_summary: The only works with stress in the title, Bliese 1988 'Metrical sequences and climax in the poetry of Joel' (OPTAT 2: 52-84), is a verse-meter/rhetorical-climax study of the book of Joel (prosody of poetry, not word-stress placement);org's Journal of Translation and Textlinguistics collection is dark, sil.org and HathiTrust behind an automated-access block, all search engines blocked); The three open sources already held by the project from the compilation of 9/16 were re-read: Prince 1975 pp.18-19 and McCarthy 1979 p.36 give the rule 'penult stress in vowel-final words, final stress otherwise' (confirms/refines the catalog's weight-hedged coding from GKC section 29), and Suchard 2016 p.100 states Tiberian stress is phonemic (minimal pairs qåmå/qåmå, bånu/bånu) while reconstructing an earlier fixed-penultimate stage. None supersedes Gesenius-Kautzsch-Cowley 1910 as the deciding descriptive source; the catalog's classification stands.

new_statements.reading: Final stress in consonant-final words; penultimate stress in vowel-final words (rule: stress the last vowel followed by at most one final vowel), with surface final stress in vowel-final forms like katb+a, katb+u attributed to deletion of the would-be stressed vowel. Same generalisation as the catalog's weight-hedged coding (final by default, penult only when the ultima is open), formalised with explicit conditions; McCarthy 1979 p.36 restates it as 'penult stress in vowel-final words and final stress otherwise', and Suchard 2016 p.100 adds that the resulting Tiberian stress is phonemic (minimal pairs).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement generalisation as the catalog's weight-hedged GKC sec. 29 coding (tone as a rule on the last syllable, less often the penult, a closed penult stressed only when the ultima is open) and as the Prince 1975 statement held by the project (final stress in consonant-final words, penult in CVV-final words), which Churchyard cites (Prince 1975:19, McCarthy 1979). Adds: the derivational level at which the rule holds (pre-epenthesis, post-suffixation), a foot-based formalisation (syllabic trochee over the last two elements counting a final extrasyllabic consonant), the full inventory of opacity sources (segholates, monophthongisation, four pausally-blocked stress shifts, nesiga), a lat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress sits in a two-syllable window at the right edge and its place is fixed by the shape of the word's end at the point of stress assignment (after all suffixation, before segholate epenthesis and before loss of final-consonant extrasyllabicity): final syllable if the word then ends in a consonant, penultimate syllable if it ends in an open long-vowel (CVV) syllable. Churchyard formalises this as one non-iterative quantity-insensitive syllabic trochee over the last two 'elements' of the word, where a word-final extrasyllabic consonant counts as an element, so stress is always on the penultimate element (pp. 15-16), recapitulating the prehistoric uniform penultimate stress (ch. 4 sec. 4.3: proto-Hebrew stress was always penultimate; after loss of word-final short vowels stress stayed on the same syllable, yielding final stress in now consonant-final words). Surface departures come from later processes: segholate epenthesis (/malk/ -> mélek with penult stress), monophthongisation creating stressed final -CVV (dibré), four stress-shift processes (rightward shift off a light penult onto final CVV with reduction; leftward shift in the consecutive imperfect; rightward shift in 2ms/1s consecutive perfect; shift in 1st/2nd sg pronouns) all blocked in pause, and the phrase-level rhythm rule (nesiga) retracting stress before an adjacent stressed word. Stress shifts may land on CVV but are blocked from landing on CVC (fn. 1.16).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec. 1.3.4.5.2 (pp. 106-107), following Dresher 1981 as modified: secondary stress is assigned late, on surface representations, and is 'an almost purely rhythmic surface phenomenon': CVVC reduction structures (single trimoraic syllables) generally receive secondary stress wherever they stand (sometimes also CVV.Cv and CV.HVC structures); otherwise every second reduction structure to the left of a stressed one receives secondary stress; with exactly three reduction structures at the start of a word the initial one is sometimes stressed instead (initial-dactyl effect, partly phrasal); word-internal reduced syllables are ignored. The Tiberian metheg grapheme marks secondary stress only inconsistently (sec. 1.4.3.2). Late secondary-stress assignment follows the rhythm rule (ch. 2 sec. 2.7).
new_statements.exceptions: One accented morpheme: the 3fs perfective -at- before a pronominal object suffix always carries stress (possible initially-assigned antepenultimate stress in -átkaa forms, fn. 1.9, p. 13); word-final 3fs verbal -aa (< /at/) is unstressed (qáamaa 'she stood up') while nominal fem. -aa is stressed (qaamáa), handled by rule ordering (fn. 1.15, pp. 14-15); some surface stressed final -CVV from underlying -VC (1sg -í < /iy/, fn. 1.14); the quasi-clitic directional suffix -aa (fn. 1.10); pausal forms block all four stress shifts and so show the default position; lamedh-he truncated jussive/consecutive-imperfect forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern Biblical Hebrew. Churchyard 1999 describes Tiberian Biblical Hebrew, i.e. the Tiberian Masoretic vocalisation and accentuation of the Hebrew Bible (the same reading tradition as the catalog's GKC record and the Prince 1975 statement), with ch. 4 on pre-Tiberian/proto-Hebrew stress history. Levinsohn 2006 draws examples from Koine Greek and Biblical Hebrew; Longacre 2006 analyses the Hebrew text of Psalm 18.

audit.recode_to: morphological (alternatively lexical): main stress confined to the last two syllables, final by default, penultimate in morphologically/lexically defined classes (segolate nouns; perfect suffixes -tā/-tī/-nū; -nā; etc.), contrastive on the surface (qā́mā 'she arose' vs qāmā́ 'standing (f.)', bā́nū 'in us' vs bānū́ 'they built'). Keep GKC 29a closure constraints as phonotactic co-occurrence restrictions in the notes, and keep the Metheg/secondary-stress and nesiga fields as they are.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three GKC sect. 29 passages and both Khan 2020 supporting passages are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated sections/pages. (2) Deciding source: GKC 1910 is a genuine reference grammar and, for a corpus language read off Masoretic accents, its facts stand; Khan 2020 (held) is the modern authority but gives no placement rule. The weak point is not the source but the classification drawn from it: GKC says 'as a rule final, less frequently penult' plus closure co-occurrence constraints and ties final stress to 'formative additions' — it does not say weight selects the stressed syllable, and the record's own test has only 8/20 marked forms obeying the formalized weight rule. (3) Sources opened now: Suchard 2016 p. 100 states outright that BH stress is phonemic with minimal pairs (contradicts a weight-predictable reading); Prince 1975 pp. 18-21 and McCarthy 1979 pp. 1

sources.note: Final stress in consonant-final words; in vowel-final words stress is penultimate (rule: stress the last vowel that is followed by at most one word-final vowel), with the apparent final stress of katb+a, katb+u derived by deleting the vowel that would have carried stress and re-stressing the next syllable. This is a formalisation of the same generalisation the catalog codes as weight-hedged (final by default, penult when the ultima is open); it refines rather than contradicts GKC section 29.

sources.quote: 'In the Leningrad Codex, the accented syllable of every prosodic word is marked by a cantillation sign. This accent may be treated as equivalent to word stress. In Biblical Hebrew, stress is phonemic, as can be seen from minimal pairs like qåmǻ 'standing' vs. qǻmå 'she stood up', bånú 'they built' vs. bǻnu 'in us'.' (then reconstructs an earlier regular-penultimate stage, sects. 4.2.3-4.2.4).

tone.quote: The other is a prosodic notion whereby free forms receive an accent (in the musical interpretation of the prosody), and dependent forms are clitics bound to a free form by a maqqef ‘hyphen’ … The Tiberian notation distinguishes two types of accents: conjunctive and disjunctive. A conjunctive accent C on a word indicates that the word is part of the same phrase as the word that follows it. A disjunctive accent Di indicates that a word is final in its phrase. … Tone Lengthening: A vowel with prosodic word stress is lengthened under certain conditions.

sources.note: The 26 te'amim graphemes 'represent pitch accents' forming the intonational contours of the verse; pitch accents are explicitly 'post-lexical movements of pitch associated with the locus of lexical stress'; the accents also mark the locus of lexical stress; proposes prosodic-word / minor-phrase / major-phrase / intonational-phrase domains (head/edge-prominence intonation system) against Dresher's 1994 LCD-based model. I.e. lexical prosody = stress; pitch is intonational, no lexical tone.

tone.quote: The graphemes of the ṭǝʿāmîm represent pitch accents, and together they form the intonational contours of the verse, indicating the proper prosodic vocalisation of the biblical text (Pitcher 2020:130-145). Generally speaking, conjunctive ṭǝʿāmîm conjoin words to form a cohesive unit, while disjunctive ṭǝʿāmîm delimit a cohesive unit. ... [fn. 5] Pitch accents are post-lexical movements of pitch associated with the locus of lexical stress. ... [p.3] 3) to indicate the locus of lexical stress, as most ṭǝʿāmîm are placed above or below the first consonant of the stressed syllable (Yeivin 1980:158).
tone.says: The 26 te'amim graphemes 'represent pitch accents' forming the intonational contours of the verse; pitch accents are explicitly 'post-lexical movements of pitch associated with the locus of lexical stress'; the accents also mark the locus of lexical stress; proposes prosodic-word / minor-phrase / major-phrase / intonational-phrase domains (head/edge-prominence intonation system) against Dresher's 1994 LCD-based model. I.e. lexical prosody = stress; pitch is intonational, no lexical tone.
